reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and breast imaging guidance
clinicalPearls: Fat necrosis is a benign inflammatory response of breast adipose tissue to injury, and it is an important mimic of carcinoma on both examination and imaging
There is often a history of trauma, breast surgery, radiotherapy, fat grafting, or anticoagulation, though the precipitating event may be forgotten
It can present as a firm, sometimes irregular lump, occasionally with skin tethering, dimpling, or bruising, closely resembling malignancy
Imaging appearances are highly variable, ranging from a benign oil cyst with a characteristic rim to spiculated masses or suspicious microcalcification that overlap with cancer
Because it can look malignant, triple assessment with core biopsy is frequently required to reach a confident benign diagnosis
An oil cyst with typical features on mammography or ultrasound may be diagnostic and avoid the need for biopsy
Most established fat necrosis needs no treatment beyond reassurance once malignancy is excluded, and it tends to settle or stabilise over time
Any lesion with persisting or discordant suspicious features should be biopsied or excised rather than assumed benign
reference.pathophysiology: Fat necrosis occurs when adipocytes are damaged by trauma, surgery, radiotherapy, or ischaemia, releasing lipid that triggers a local inflammatory reaction. Macrophages and giant cells engulf the released fat, and the process evolves through acute inflammation, the formation of lipid-laden oil cysts, and eventual fibrosis and dystrophic calcification. The resulting scarring can distort surrounding tissue and tether the skin, while the calcification and architectural change on imaging can closely imitate carcinoma. The variable stage of evolution explains the wide spectrum of clinical and radiological appearances.
additionalDifferentials: Fibroadenoma or other benign solid lump
Radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination and history for trauma, surgery, or radiotherapy as part of triple assessment
Mammography, which may show an oil cyst, calcification, or a suspicious mass
Core needle biopsy where imaging or clinical features are not clearly benign
Magnetic resonance imaging in selected cases when other imaging is indeterminate
Interval imaging follow-up when a lesion is presumed benign but not biopsied
redFlags: Spiculated mass or suspicious microcalcification that could represent carcinoma
Skin tethering or dimpling without a clear benign explanation
A lesion that enlarges or fails to settle over time
reference.prognosis: Fat necrosis is benign with an excellent prognosis; once cancer is excluded, most lesions stabilise, resolve, or persist as an inert scar or oil cyst, and it carries no increased risk of malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a lump is fat necrosis on the basis of trauma history alone and missing a coincidental carcinoma
Failing to biopsy imaging features that overlap with malignancy
Ignoring discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathological findings
Attributing skin tethering to fat necrosis without adequate assessment
Not arranging follow-up for a presumed benign but unbiopsied lesion
references: Standard breast surgery reference text on benign breast disease
Breast imaging guidance on benign mimics of malignancy
management: Confirm the benign diagnosis with triple assessment, using core needle biopsy where imaging or examination is not clearly benign
Reassure and manage conservatively once malignancy is excluded, as most lesions stabilise, resolve or persist as an inert oil cyst
Provide simple analgesia and supportive measures such as warm compresses for tenderness
Aspirate a symptomatic oil cyst or surgically excise a persistent, enlarging or troublesome mass
Arrange interval imaging follow-up when a lesion is presumed benign but not biopsied
Review the precipitating factor such as trauma, surgery, radiotherapy, fat grafting or anticoagulation, and reassure that there is no increased cancer risk
